IndusTech Corporation - Q3 2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the IndusTech Corporation Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are in listen-only mode. After the presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. If you would like to ask a question at that time, please press * then 1 on your telephone keypad. If your question has been answered or you would like to remove yourself from the queue, please press the # key. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Sarah Thompson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson (Head of Investor Relations):
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss IndusTech Corporation's results for the third quarter of 2024. Joining me on today's call are Michael Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer; John Ramirez, Chief Financial Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Operating Officer; and Dr. Alex Patel, Chief Technology Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking in nature and subject to certain risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Michael Reynolds.

Michael Reynolds (CEO):
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on IndusTech Corporation's performance for the third quarter. We've made significant progress on several fronts, and I'd like to highlight a few key achievements. First, our automation and digital offerings delivered exceptional growth, driving efficiency gains across the manufacturing value chain. Second, we maintained our strong dividend policy, continuing our streak as a Dividend Aristocrat with an attractive yield. Third, our guidance is supported by solid assumptions on economic growth and end-market demand. Fourth, favorable price-cost dynamics boosted our margins despite raw material pressures. Fifth, end markets show promising growth outlook in the near and medium term. Sixth, we're providing raised revenue guidance for Q4 and full-year 2025. Seventh, gross and operating margins continued their upward trends. Eighth, order intake and book-to-bill ratios strengthened across key end markets like construction, mining, and agriculture.

We are confident that our strategic initiatives are positioning us for long-term sustainable growth.

Now, I'll turn the call over to John Ramirez to provide more detail on our financial results.

John Ramirez (CFO):
Thank you, Michael. Turning to our financial performance, IndusTech Corporation reported $2.36 billion in revenue for the third quarter, representing a 15% increase year-over-year. Gross margin was 32.4%, driven by pricing discipline, favorable product mix, and moderating input costs. Operating expenses were $500 million, resulting in an operating income of $285 million. Our net income for the quarter was $210 million, or $1.85 per share.

Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for joining our third quarter earnings call. Before I dive deeper into segment details, I'd like to spend a few minutes on one of our key growth engines: our automation and digital offerings portfolio. This segment not only drove outsized performance this quarter but is fundamentally transforming efficiency across the manufacturing value chain—for our customers and for IndusTech.

Let me start with the numbers. In Q3, our Automation and Digital Solutions segment delivered $1.28 billion in revenue, up 27% year-over-year and 8% sequentially. That's ahead of our guidance midpoint and represents the 11th straight quarter of double-digit growth. Drilling down, hardware—think our next-gen PLCs like the IndusFlex 5000 series and collaborative robots integrated with our CobotAI platform—grew 22% to $850 million. But the real standout was our digital offerings: software, IIoT connectivity, and analytics services surged 42% to $430 million, now comprising 34% of segment revenue, up from 28% a year ago. Recurring revenue from our SaaS-based Digital Factory Suite hit $185 million, a 55% jump, with ARR now at $720 million—giving us a robust 75% gross margin profile in this high-margin sub-segment.

This growth isn't happening in a vacuum; it's fueled by secular tailwinds in the industrial equipment space. We're seeing accelerated adoption of Industry 4.0 technologies amid the global push for smart factories. Take the EV battery manufacturing boom—our automation systems are now standard in gigafactory lines from players like CATL and Panasonic, where we've deployed over 150 digital twin-enabled production lines this year. Similarly, in semiconductors, demand from TSMC and Intel fabs has spiked our order intake for edge-computing gateways, up 35% YoY.

Now, on the efficiency impact—this is where we create real customer value and sticky, annuity-like revenue. Our solutions are delivering measurable ROI: customers using our Predictive Maintenance AI, powered by machine learning models trained on 10 petabytes of anonymized factory data, are seeing MTBF improvements of 25-30% and unplanned downtime reductions of 18%. For instance, a major Tier 1 automotive supplier in the Midwest reported OEE gains of 22% after integrating our SCADA-over-5G platform, translating to $12 million in annual savings per plant. Overall, across our 2,500+ active digital deployments, we're tracking average throughput increases of 15% and energy efficiency gains of 12-15%—critical in this era of rising power costs and ESG mandates.

Regionally, the story is strong everywhere but differentiated. North America led with 32% growth, driven by reshoring and the CHIPS Act; we've secured $450 million in backlog from U.S. hyperscalers building AI data center cooling systems. EMEA grew 24%, bolstered by EU Green Deal subsidies for retrofitting legacy plants—think Siemens-like partnerships where we're co-developing brownfield automation upgrades. APAC was up 28%, with China and Southeast Asia leading on high-mix, low-volume electronics assembly; our robotics orders there jumped 40% on labor shortages.

Strategically, we're leaning in hard. We've ramped R&D to 8.5% of segment sales, investing $110 million this quarter in generative AI for process optimization—imagine autonomous recipe tuning that rivals Rockwell's FactoryTalk but with 40% faster convergence. We've also expanded our ecosystem: new alliances with AWS for hybrid cloud-edge analytics and NVIDIA for GPU-accelerated vision systems in our inspection robots. This positions us to capture the $150 billion IIoT market opportunity by 2028, per McKinsey estimates, where digital services could hit 50% of our mix.

Looking forward, our Q4 guide calls for 25-28% segment growth, with backlog at a record $2.7 billion—2.1x book-to-bill. Margins should expand another 150 basis points to 42% as digital scales. We're not just riding the automation wave; we're engineering it for our customers' competitiveness and our sustained high-teens EPS growth.

Moving now to our capital allocation framework, particularly our dividend policy and yield, which remains a cornerstone of our shareholder returns strategy here at IndusTech. As many of you know, IndusTech has proudly increased its dividend for 28 consecutive years, earning our place among the elite Dividend Aristocrats in the industrials sector—much like longstanding peers such as Illinois Tool Works and Dover Corporation. This track record underscores our commitment to delivering consistent, growing cash returns to shareholders, even through the cyclical headwinds that define our manufacturing and industrial equipment industry.

Let me start with the numbers. For fiscal 2024, we declared a quarterly dividend of $0.66 per share, equating to an annualized payout of $2.64. This represents a 10% increase over the prior year's $2.40, aligning with our long-term policy of targeting 8-12% annual dividend growth, gated by sustainable earnings power. At yesterday's closing stock price of $98.50, this delivers a forward dividend yield of 2.68%—attractive relative to the S&P 500 Industrials Index average of 1.8% and our direct comps like Caterpillar at 1.6% and Cummins at 2.2%. Our trailing 12-month payout ratio stands at a prudent 42% of adjusted EPS of $6.28, well within our stated target range of 40-50%. This leaves ample dry powder for reinvestment, with free cash flow conversion exceeding 95% in Q3, driven by our optimized working capital management amid stabilizing supply chains.

Our dividend policy is deliberately conservative yet progressive, designed to weather the volatility inherent in our end-markets—construction, mining, agriculture, and OEM equipment. We benchmark against core industrial capex cycles, where orders for our heavy earthmoving kit like the IndusTech HX-500 hydraulic excavators and our precision CNC machining centers correlate tightly with ISM Manufacturing PMI readings above 50. In 2024, despite a softer capex environment with U.S. non-residential construction starts down 8% YoY per Census Bureau data, our policy held firm: we stress-tested distributions against a hypothetical 20% EPS downturn, similar to the 2020 pandemic trough, and maintained coverage ratios north of 2.0x.

Looking regionally, this discipline paid off. In North America, which accounted for 52% of our $4.2 billion revenue, dividend sustainability was bolstered by the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act tailwinds—IIJA funding has juiced demand for our road milling and asphalt pavers, with backlog up 15% to $1.8 billion. Europe, at 22% of mix, faced headwinds from the energy crisis and destocking in wind turbine components, capping our regional EPS contribution at 18% versus 25% in 2023; yet, our yield remains compelling for income-focused European investors amid ECB rate hikes. APAC, our growth engine at 26% of revenue, saw robust uptake of automation solutions like our RoboForge robotic welding systems in China's EV battery gigafactories, supporting a 12% dividend growth clip there.

Strategically, we're balancing this shareholder-friendly policy with aggressive technical initiatives to drive future payout capacity. We've allocated $450 million—or 11% of 2024 capex—to Industry 4.0 upgrades, including digital twin simulations for our gas turbine aftermarket services and IoT-enabled predictive maintenance on forklift fleets, which boosted equipment uptime 22% and aftermarket margins to 28%. This positions us ahead of the electrification curve; for instance, our new eHX-300 battery-electric excavator, compliant with EU Stage V emissions and IRA tax credits, is ramping to 20% of NA excavator sales by 2025. We're also eyeing bolt-on M&A, like our recent $180 million tuck-in of a German precision tooling firm, funded 70% from FCF to preserve dividend headroom.

In summary, our 2.68% yield, backed by fortress-like balance sheet metrics—Net Debt/EBITDA at 1.2x and $1.1 billion in liquidity—offers a compelling entry point ahead of an anticipated industrials capex inflection. We expect to announce our Q1 dividend next month, targeting another mid-single-digit hike, contingent on Board approval.

Today, I'd like to dive deep into the impact of price-cost dynamics on our margins, which was a key driver of our outperformance this quarter. As you know, in the industrial equipment sector, where we design and manufacture heavy-duty CNC machining centers, hydraulic presses, and precision forging equipment for OEMs in automotive, aerospace, and energy end-markets, managing input cost volatility against pricing discipline is mission-critical. Our gross margins expanded 290 basis points year-over-year to 32.4%, reaching the high end of our long-term target range of 30-34%. This reflects proactive pricing actions more than offsetting raw material headwinds, bolstered by operational efficiencies.

First, on the cost side: Raw material inflation remained a persistent challenge, though it's showing signs of stabilization. Our basket of key inputs—primarily structural steel, aluminum alloys like 6061-T6, copper for electrical components, and specialty forgings—rose approximately 12% year-over-year in Q3, down from a peak of 22% in Q1 2023. Steel prices, tracked via the CRU North America Hot-Rolled Coil Index, averaged $850 per short ton, up 8% sequentially due to lingering effects from the Ukraine conflict disrupting Black Sea exports and U.S. mill capacity rationalizations by players like Nucor and Steel Dynamics. Aluminum hit $2,450 per metric ton on the LME, pressured by energy surcharges amid volatile natural gas prices in Europe. Copper, critical for our servo motors and wiring harnesses, surged 15% YoY to $9,200 per tonne, exacerbated by supply constraints from Chilean mine strikes and Chinese smelter cuts.

Regionally, this played out differently. In North America, which accounts for 55% of our revenue, costs were up 10% but mitigated by our Midwest steel mill partnerships, where we've locked in 70% of 2024 volumes via quarterly collars hedging against CRU index swings. In EMEA, representing 25% of sales, costs inflated 18% due to EU carbon border adjustment mechanisms (CBAM) adding $50-70 per ton to imported steel from Asia. APAC, our 20% exposure, saw milder 7% inflation thanks to localized sourcing from POSCO in Korea for our forging dies, though logistics surcharges from Red Sea disruptions added 2-3% to landed costs.

Now, turning to pricing actions, which have been our margin tailwind. We successfully implemented broad-based price increases averaging 9% across our portfolio, with full-year capture now at 85% of targeted $180 million in revenue uplift. In our core CNC lathe and milling machine lines, we achieved 10-12% realizations, customer-accepted due to our tech-differentiated features like AI-driven predictive maintenance via our IndusAI platform, which delivers 15% uptime gains versus legacy competitors like Haas Automation. Hydraulic press pricing rose 8%, supported by aerospace OEM contracts with Boeing and Airbus suppliers emphasizing our high-pressure servo tech. Value-based pricing has been key here—rather than commoditized list pricing, we've tied 40% of increases to total cost of ownership (TCO) models, showcasing 20% energy savings from our variable-frequency drive upgrades.

Customer pushback was minimal, at under 5% volume loss, concentrated in spot-market discrete parts for non-contracted ag equipment buyers. This compares favorably to peers like Caterpillar, who reported 7% pricing in their resource industries segment, or Ingersoll Rand, at 6% in precision tech. Our 18-month backlog, up 14% YoY to $2.8 billion, provides visibility, with 60% contracted at elevated prices.

Net price-cost: Pricing outpaced costs by 450 basis points in Q3, driving the gross margin expansion I mentioned. Adjusted for mix—favorably impacted by higher-margin aerospace forgings at 38% margins versus industrial at 28%—our underlying price-cost favorability was $65 million, or 320 bps of expansion. Factory absorption helped too, running at 92% utilization across our six U.S. and two European plants, leveraging LEAN initiatives like single-minute exchange of dies (SMED) to cut changeover times 25%.

Strategically, we're future-proofing with three initiatives. One, supply chain resilience: We've derisked 30% of steel exposure via vertical integration, commissioning a mini-mill in Ohio with electric arc furnace (EAF) tech using scrap feeds, targeting first steel in Q2 2025 at 20% below spot. Two, advanced materials substitution: Piloting titanium aluminides in select aerospace presses to reduce weight 15% and aluminum dependency, partnering with Aperam for prototyping. Three, dynamic pricing analytics: Our ERP-integrated model, powered by SAP Ariba and machine learning, forecasts input indices weekly, enabling real-time contract adjustments—already capturing 2 extra points of pricing in APAC.

Looking forward, we expect raw material costs to trough in Q1 2025 with steel stabilizing at $800-850/ton, assuming no major geopolitical flares. We'll layer on another 5-7% pricing in Q4, targeting gross margins of 33% for FY25, with EBITDA margins hitting 22%. This positions us well amid softening industrial capex—U.S. ISM PMI at 47 signaling caution—but our aftermarket services, up 22% YoY with 45% margins, provide a buffer.

I'll now turn to our margin performance, which continues to reflect the strength of our operational execution amid a dynamic industrial landscape. As you know, in the manufacturing and industrial equipment sector—where we've seen peers like Caterpillar and Deere navigating similar headwinds from volatile steel and aluminum pricing, supply chain disruptions, and softening demand in cyclical end-markets like construction and mining—margins are a critical barometer of pricing discipline, cost leverage, and portfolio mix.

Starting with gross margin: For the quarter, we delivered a robust expansion of 220 basis points year-over-year to 28.5%, marking our sixth consecutive quarter of sequential improvement. This brings our trailing twelve-month gross margin to 27.8%, up from 24.9% a year ago. On a sequential basis, we gained another 50 basis points from Q2's 28.0%. Let me break down the key drivers here, as they're emblematic of the strategic levers we've pulled across our portfolio of heavy machinery, material handling equipment, and precision automation systems.

First, pricing remains our North Star. We realized a 5.2% increase in average selling prices (ASPs) year-over-year, driven by targeted actions on our core product lines, including our flagship IndusForge excavators and the next-gen IntelliLift palletizers. This was partially offset by a modest 1.8% volume decline, tied to softer capex from mining OEMs amid lower commodity prices for copper and iron ore. Importantly, our pricing gains held firm despite competitive pressures from low-cost Asian imports, thanks to our "value-based selling" framework, which emphasizes uptime guarantees and IoT-enabled predictive maintenance—features that resonate strongly with customers prioritizing total cost of ownership over sticker price.

Second, cost of goods sold (COGS) headwinds moderated significantly. Raw material costs, which peaked at 15% above 2023 averages last year due to the Ukraine conflict's ripple effects on global steel supply, declined 3.1% quarter-over-quarter as contracts with key suppliers like Nucor and ArcelorMittal reset at lower spot rates. Freight expenses dropped 12% sequentially, benefiting from normalized ocean rates post the Red Sea disruptions and our shift to nearshoring strategies in Mexico under USMCA. Factory labor efficiencies improved via our Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) upgrade and deployment of collaborative robots (cobots) from partners like Universal Robots, boosting labor productivity by 7% and lifting utilization rates to 85% across our U.S. and European plants—well above the industry benchmark of 78% per recent Deloitte industrials reports.

Product mix was another tailwind, contributing roughly 80 basis points to the expansion. Aftermarket parts and services, which carry gross margins north of 45%, now represent 32% of total revenue, up from 28% a year ago. This shift is fueled by our IndusGuard subscription model for connected equipment, which saw 25% YoY growth as fleet managers extend asset life amid high interest rates curbing new machine buys. Conversely, lower-margin commodity conveyors dipped as a mix percentage.

Regionally, the picture is bifurcated but positive overall. North America, our largest market at 52% of sales, drove the margin beat with 32.1% gross margins—bolstered by Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) funded projects spurring demand for our road-building and aggregates equipment. EMEA lagged at 24.8%, pressured by energy costs and a 10% drop in German machinery orders per VDMA data, though our diversification into renewables like wind turbine handlers is gaining traction. Asia-Pacific held steady at 25.3%, with strength in India offsetting China softness from real estate overhang.

Turning to operating margins: We expanded 160 basis points year-over-year to 12.1%, with adjusted operating income of $285 million on $2.36 billion in revenue. Sequential expansion was 40 basis points. OpEx as a percentage of sales declined to 16.4% from 17.2% YoY, reflecting disciplined cost management. SG&A came in 2% below plan through zero-based budgeting and headcount optimization—net headcount flat despite 4% wage inflation—while R&D investments ticked up to 4.1% of sales, focused on digital twins and AI-driven quality control via our partnership with Siemens Xcelerator platform. This positions us ahead of peers; for context, our operating margin now exceeds Caterpillar's recent quarterly print by 110 basis points and aligns with Ingersoll Rand's premium segment performance.

Strategically, these trends underscore our "Margin First" playbook: We've accelerated value analysis/value engineering (VAVE) initiatives, targeting 2-3% annual COGS reductions through design-for-manufacturability on platforms like our modular skid-steer loaders. Supply chain resilience is key—we've reduced China exposure from 22% to 15% of direct materials, ramping Vietnam and Eastern Europe footprints. And on the tech front, our Industry 4.0 roadmap, including 5G-enabled edge computing for real-time OEE monitoring, is delivering 1-2% quarterly margin accretion.

Looking forward, we expect gross margins to hold in the 28-29% band for Q4, with operating margins expanding another 50-75 basis points, assuming stable steel pricing around $650/ton and no major FX volatility—the dollar's strength has already added 30 basis points to margins via translation gains. Risks remain from potential tariffs or renewed labor shortages, but our $1.2 billion in backlog—up 8% YoY with strong aftermarket weighting—provides visibility.

Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for joining our Q3 earnings call for Global Industrial Equipment Corp., or as we know it, IndusTech, your leading provider of heavy-duty machinery and integrated solutions for construction, mining, agriculture, and beyond. Today, I'd like to dive deep into our order intake dynamics and book-to-bill trends, segmented by end market. This remains a cornerstone metric for our visibility into future revenue streams, backlog growth, and overall demand health in the cyclical industrial equipment sector.

Starting with the big picture: In Q3, total order intake reached $2.85 billion, up 18% year-over-year and 12% sequentially from Q2. This marks our strongest quarterly bookings since Q4 2022, driven by robust capex recovery across core markets. Our trailing 12-month book-to-bill ratio stands at 1.22x, reflecting healthy backlog expansion to $12.4 billion—up 25% YoY—with approximately 14 months of forward visibility at current run rates. Aftermarket and services orders, which now comprise 28% of total intake, grew 22% YoY, underscoring the sticky revenue from our installed base of over 1.2 million machines globally.

Now, let's break this down by end market, where we saw differentiated performance reflecting unique macro tailwinds, regional variances, and our strategic execution on next-gen products like our electric excavators and autonomous haul trucks.

Construction End Market (42% of Q3 Orders)  
Construction remains our largest segment, with Q3 orders of $1.2 billion, surging 24% YoY and 15% QoQ. Book-to-bill here expanded to 1.35x, fueled by pent-up demand from infrastructure megaprojects. In the Americas, which accounted for 55% of segment orders, we're seeing outsized gains from U.S. IIJA funding—think data center builds and highway expansions akin to what Caterpillar has capitalized on. Our IndusTech 390F electric excavators, with zero-emission capabilities compliant with California's CARB standards, captured 30% market share in urban jobsites, driving a 40% YoY order spike for hybrid and electric models.

EMEA was mixed: Strong in Germany and the Nordics on wind farm groundwork, up 20% YoY, but softer in the UK due to lingering labor shortages. Asia-Pacific shone with 28% YoY growth, led by India's $1.3 trillion National Infrastructure Pipeline; our partnerships with Larsen & Toubro have secured multi-year wheel loader frameworks. Strategically, we're investing $250 million in FY24 to scale production of telematics-enabled dozers at our Peoria facility, enhancing fleet optimization via our IndusTech Connect platform—early adopters report 15% uptime gains, converting pilots to full orders.

Mining End Market (28% of Q3 Orders)  
Mining orders hit $795 million, up a stellar 32% YoY and 20% QoQ, with book-to-bill at 1.45x—the highest in our portfolio. This reflects the commodity supercycle: Copper prices hovering at $4.50/lb and iron ore above $120/tonne have reignited capex, mirroring BHP and Rio Tinto's aggressive expansion plans. Our ultra-class 797F autonomous haul trucks saw orders double YoY, comprising 25% of segment intake, thanks to Level 4 autonomy validated in Pilbara trials—reducing operator costs by 30% and boosting productivity 18%.

Regionally, APAC dominated at 48% of orders, with Indonesia's nickel boom and Australia's lithium rush; we've locked in $400 million in backlog from Freeport-McMoRan equivalents. The Americas contributed 35%, buoyed by Nevada gold projects, while EMEA grew 15% on Scandinavian copper. A key initiative is our battery-electric underground loader fleet, now in production at our Tampere plant, targeting ESG-mandated Tier 4 Final compliance. We're also pursuing bolt-on M&A, like our recent acquisition of a Swedish crushing tech firm, to fortify aftermarket parts for SAG mills, where margins exceed 45%.

Agriculture End Market (18% of Q3 Orders)  
Ag orders totaled $513 million, up 12% YoY but flat QoQ, with book-to-bill steady at 1.10x. Precision ag demand is accelerating amid grain prices stabilizing at $6/bushel for corn, but dealer destocking capped growth—similar to Deere's recent playbook. High-horsepower tractors (>300 HP) and self-propelled forage harvesters drove 25% of orders, led by our New Holland CR12.90 models with AI-yield mapping.

North America was the powerhouse at 60% share, up 18% YoY on farm income resilience despite Midwest floods. Brazil's soybean harvest delays boosted LATAM orders 22%, while EMEA faced headwinds from EU fertilizer curbs, down 5% but offset by precision sprayer uptake. Our strategic push includes $150 million in R&D for autonomous tractors, with beta tests at John Deere-level precision showing 20% fuel savings; we've secured OEM supply deals with AGCO partners. Long-term, we're eyeing electrification for smaller orchards, aligning with USDA sustainability grants.

Other End Markets (12% of Q3 Orders)  
Rounding out, Oil & Gas/Upstream orders grew 15% YoY to $220 million (book-to-bill 1.15x), buoyed by Permian rig counts at 450+; our FracSand pumps are winning share from Halliburton. Power Generation and Infrastructure added $122 million, up 10%, with gas turbine ancillaries benefiting from LNG export ramps in Qatar and the U.S. Gulf Coast.

Forward Outlook and Strategic Insights  
Looking ahead, we expect Q4 book-to-bill to hold in the 1.15x-1.25x range, with backlog conversion at 28% of Q4 revenue. Risks include China real estate drag on construction (only 8% of our exposure) and potential Fed pauses curbing U.S. capex. But tailwinds abound: Global mining capex projected at $150 billion in 2024 per Wood Mackenzie, U.S. farm bill extensions, and EU Green Deal subsidies.

Strategically, we're leaner and meaner—supply chain localization has cut lead times 25% via nearshoring to Mexico, and our $500 million share repurchase underscores confidence. We've launched 'IndusTech Forward,' a $1 billion multi-year initiative blending autonomy, electrification (target: 30% battery portfolio by 2027), and digital services—already lifting order premiums 8-12%. Competitively, we're outpacing Komatsu in autonomy and CNH in ag precision, positioning IndusTech for mid-teens EPS growth through the cycle.

Thank you, Michael, and good morning, everyone. As we wrap up our Q3 results, I'd like to dive into our outlook for end-market growth across our key verticals in the Manufacturing and Industrial Equipment sector. We're entering a structurally favorable period driven by secular tailwinds like reshoring, digital transformation, and the energy transition. Our visibility remains strong, with a $4.2 billion backlog up 18% year-over-year, and customer capex plans signaling sustained demand. Let me break this down by near-term—through calendar '25—and medium-term horizons out to '28, with segment-specific color.

Near-Term Outlook (CY '24-'25): Moderately Accelerating Growth Amid Selective Recovery

We project overall end-market growth of 5-7% globally in '24, ramping to 7-9% in '25, outpacing the broader 3-4% ISM Manufacturing PMI expansion we've seen. This is underpinned by OEM capex normalization post-COVID destocking, with aftermarket services—now 42% of our revenue—growing at 8-10% as utilization rates hit 82% across our customer base.

- Semiconductor and Electronics (25% of sales): This remains our brightest spot, with +12-15% growth in '24-'25. AI-driven hyperscaler investments are fueling fab expansions—think TSMC's Arizona Fab 21 and Intel's Ohio megasite under the CHIPS Act. We're seeing pull-ins for advanced lithography and deposition tools, with etch and deposition segments up 20% YoY. Backlog here is up 25%, and we're prioritizing deliveries of our next-gen plasma etch systems.

- Aerospace & Defense (20% of sales): +8-10% growth, as commercial airframe production rebounds. Boeing and Airbus are targeting 35% output ramps by '25 per their guidance, driving demand for precision CNC machining centers and automated assembly lines. Defense tailwinds from F-35 sustainment and hypersonics add upside, though supply chain frictions in forgings persist.

- Renewable Energy & Power Generation (15% of sales): +15-18% clip, led by onshore wind and utility-scale solar. U.S. IRA tax credits are accelerating turbine upgrades—Vestas and GE Vernova alone plan $2B+ in capex—and we're booking orders for our high-efficiency gearbox assemblies and blade molding equipment. Offshore wind faces permitting delays, capping that sub-segment at +10%.

- Automotive & EV (18% of sales): More challenged at +3-5%, with ICE production flatlining amid EV transition pains. Battery gigafactory builds—e.g., Tesla's Nevada expansion and LG's U.S. sites—provide offsets, boosting stamping and welding automation demand by 12%. We're de-emphasizing legacy auto here, focusing on structural battery frame lines.

- General Industrial, Oil & Gas, and Mining (22% of sales): +4-6%, with mining capex rebounding on copper demand for electrification (Rio Tinto and BHP targeting 10% fleet modernization). Oil & gas drilling efficiency gains support frac pump rebuilds, but LNG export delays temper upstream growth.

Regionally, North America drives 60% of our growth at +8-10%, fueled by reshoring—$200B+ in announced manufacturing capex per Reshoring Initiative data. Europe lags at +4-6% due to energy costs and automotive weakness, but the Green Deal's €1T investment pipeline supports renewables. Asia-Pacific ex-China grows +7-9%, with India's PLI schemes mirroring our U.S. success; China itself is flat at +2-3% amid property overhang.

Medium-Term Outlook (CY '26-'28): Structural Reacceleration to 8-11% CAGR

Looking out to '28, we see end-market expansion accelerating to an 8-11% CAGR, driven by megatrends in automation, electrification, and sustainability. This aligns with McKinsey's forecast for Industry 4.0 capex doubling to $500B annually by 2030.

Key drivers:

- Digital Factory Adoption: 60-70% of OEMs plan IoT and AI retrofits by '28, per Deloitte. Our EdgeConnect predictive maintenance platform—integrated with Rockwell Automation's FactoryTalk—positions us for +20% growth in smart machining centers, reducing downtime by 25% in pilots.

- Electrification Wave: EV and grid infrastructure demand surges +15% CAGR. We're investing $150M in capacity for e-drive assembly lines, targeting partnerships like our JV with Magna for 800V architectures.

- Sustainability Mandates: ESG compliance drives +12% in low-emission equipment. Think hydrogen-ready turbines and recycled-material CNCs; EU CBAM tariffs will accelerate this.

Challenges include tariff volatility and labor shortages, but our 85% U.S. manufacturing footprint mitigates reshoring risks. Strategically, we're allocating 12% of capex to R&D in cobot integration and additive manufacturing hybrids—e.g., binder jetting for titanium aerospace parts—while pursuing tuck-in M&A like our recent $200M acquisition of a precision grinding specialist to verticalize supply chains.

In summary, our end markets are poised for multi-year growth, with semiconductors and renewables as lead indicators. We maintain FY'25 guidance for 10-12% organic revenue growth and 18-20% EPS expansion, assuming no recession.

Before I turn it back, let me walk you through our revenue guidance for the fourth quarter of fiscal 2024 and the full fiscal year 2025. We're pleased with the momentum we're seeing across our core segments—precision CNC machining centers, automated material handling systems, and our growing robotics and IoT-enabled equipment portfolio—as industrial capex cycles continue to inflect positively amid reshoring trends and the push toward smart factories.

Starting with Q4, we are guiding to revenue of $1.25 billion to $1.30 billion, representing growth of 7% to 10% year-over-year and roughly flat to 3% sequential growth from Q3. This outlook reflects a strong book-to-bill ratio of 1.15x entering the quarter, driven by backlog conversion on high-margin OEM orders. Key tailwinds include:

- North America, which we expect to contribute about 45% of Q4 revenue, up mid-teens YoY, fueled by CHIPS Act-related semi fab builds and EV battery gigafactory expansions. We've seen particular strength in orders for our next-gen 5-axis CNC mills from customers like Intel's Ohio fab and Tesla's Nevada expansion—similar to the demand patterns peers like Applied Materials are reporting.
